questions.title: What standard does the Fifth Circuit use for reviewing a denial of Judgment as a Matter of Law (JMOL) in patent cases?
questions.question_body: I see that the opinion says the Fifth Circuit reviews denials of JMOL de novo, but I’m struggling to understand what that actually means for a patent infringement case. Does the appellate court get to re‑examine every element of the jury’s finding, or does it only look at the legal conclusion? How does this de‑novo standard differ from the standard used for reviewing factual findings or from the standards applied in other circuits?

questions.title: In the ’775’ patent, why does the court treat ‘S1, S2 and S3’ as ‘separately identifiable’ but not ‘unique’, and how does that affect claim scope after amendment?
questions.question_body: The opinion discusses that the district court construed the claim limitation that the three signals must be separately identifiable but not unique, allowing the accused radio to use two signals and a copy of one. I’m unclear on what the difference is between ‘separately identifiable’ and ‘unique’. Why doesn’t the court treat three distinct physical signals as a requirement? Also, the court says the amendment from ‘two or three signals’ to ‘three signals’ does not amount to surrendering claim scope – how is that conclusion reached?

questions.title: When an expert’s testimony is contradictory, can a court still find evidence sufficient for a JMOL, and what are the principles that guide that decision?
questions.question_body: Dr. Wells gave conflicting statements about whether the RF ADC sampled the modeled PIM path. The court calls his testimony self‑contradictory and therefore insufficient for a jury verdict. What rules govern when expert testimony that contains contradictions is admissible for a JMOL? Are there specific standards for consistency, clarity, or sufficiency that a court must apply?

questions.title: Why did the court find the accused radios did not perform the seven claimed multiplications in the ‘775’ patent, and what evidence is necessary to show a design meets such a multiplication requirement?
questions.question_body: The opinion says the Nokia document lists only three distinct multiplications and does not show all seven claimed calculations. How does the court determine that the accused radio does not meet the seven‑multiplication requirement? Is it enough that the data sheet or internal document only shows fewer multiplications, or does the court need direct evidence that each of the seven is performed? What kind of expert testimony or engineering documentation would satisfy the court’s standard?

questions.title: What is the practical application of the ‘substantial evidence’ standard in infringement findings, and how does it differ from the preponderance standard?
questions.question_body: The opinion states that the jury’s infringement verdict was not supported by substantial evidence. I’m used to the preponderance-of‑evidence standard in civil cases – how is substantial evidence different? Does the court require a higher burden from the plaintiff, or does it simply look for a stronger factual basis for the claim? How does the ‘substantial evidence’ test interact with the evidence presented by expert witnesses?

questions.title: How does the Fifth Circuit apply an abuse‑of‑discretion standard when reviewing a district court’s denial of a new trial on damages in a patent case?
questions.question_body: The opinion mentions that the court reviewed the denial of a new trial on damages for abuse of discretion. I’m not clear on what that standard looks like—what does the appellate court examine? Must the district court have made a clear error, or is any misstep enough? Does this standard apply the same way when damages are decided by a judge versus a jury?

questions.title: What is the difference between internal and external passive intermodulation (PIM) in the context of the ‘134’ patent, and why is that distinction significant?
questions.question_body: The background section explains that internal PIM stems from inside the radio and external PIM comes from outside sources. I don’t understand how that distinction affects the infringement analysis. Does it change what signals must be sampled, or what claim elements are required? Why does the court focus on the ADC sampling both the signal of interest and the interference‑generating signals?

questions.title: How does the remaining life of a patent factor into lump‑sum damages, and does a new trial on damages require a new infringement trial?
questions.question_body: The jury awarded $166,303,391 in lump‑sum damages based on the remaining life of the patents. I’m unsure how the court connects patent life to damages. Also, if the appellate court vacates the damages award and orders a new trial on damages, must the infringement verdict also be revisited, or can damages be recalculated based on the same finding of infringement?
